paragraphs.heading: What it was
paragraphs.text: The Space Shuttle was a spacecraft system that NASA, the US space agency, flew from 1981 to 2011. It was partly reusable, and it worked in low Earth orbit, including trips to the International Space Station. Its formal name was the Space Transportation System, or STS. That name came from a 1969 plan, led by vice president Spiro Agnew, for a set of reusable spacecraft, and the shuttle was the one piece of that plan that got money for development.

paragraphs.heading: The fleet
paragraphs.text: Six orbiters were built in all. The first, Enterprise, was finished in 1976 and used for approach and landing tests, but it had no ability to reach orbit. Four working orbiters followed: Columbia, Challenger, Discovery and Atlantis. A fifth, Endeavour, was built in 1991 to replace Challenger. Together the five flew 135 missions, all launched from Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

paragraphs.heading: How a launch worked
paragraphs.text: The system had three main parts. The orbiter carried three RS-25 main engines, there were two recoverable solid rocket boosters, and an external tank that was not reused held liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen to feed those engines. At launch the whole stack rose straight up like an ordinary rocket, with the boosters and the main engines firing together. The boosters dropped away first, before orbit. After the main engines shut down, the tank was dropped too, and the orbiter's two Orbital Maneuvering System engines finished the climb into orbit.

paragraphs.heading: Coming home
paragraphs.text: To come home, the orbiter fired those same maneuvering engines to drop out of orbit. Thermal protection tiles shielded it as it came back into the atmosphere, and it then glided like a plane to a runway. Landings were usually at Kennedy Space Center or at Edwards Air Force Base in California. After an Edwards landing, the orbiter rode back to Florida on top of a specially modified Boeing 747.

paragraphs.heading: What it did
paragraphs.text: Shuttle missions put many satellites and space probes into orbit, including the Hubble Space Telescope. Crews ran science experiments in orbit and flew joint missions with Russia under the Shuttle-Mir program. They also helped build and service the International Space Station. Across the whole fleet, the shuttles spent 1,323 days on missions.

paragraphs.heading: Losses and retirement
paragraphs.text: Two orbiters were lost in accidents: Challenger in 1986 and Columbia in 2003. Fourteen astronauts died in the two disasters. The three that were left were retired after Atlantis made the last flight on July 21, 2011. From then until the Crew Dragon Demo-2 mission in May 2020, the United States depended on Russia's Soyuz spacecraft to carry its astronauts to the space station.

paragraphs.heading: Earlier ideas
paragraphs.text: The wish for a reusable spacecraft is older than the shuttle. In the 1950s the US Air Force proposed a reusable piloted glider for military work, and in the late 1950s it began developing a partly reusable craft called the X-20 Dyna-Soar. Rising costs and the priority given to Project Gemini ended it in December 1963. NASA and the Air Force also tested lifting bodies, aircraft that got most of their lift from their bodies rather than from wings. Those tests explored features later built into the shuttle, such as landing without power from a great height and speed.

paragraphs.heading: Choosing a shape
paragraphs.text: Engineers then argued over how much of the system should be reusable. Many liked a fully reusable design, hoping to save on hardware. NASA engineer Max Faget patented a two-stage version with a straight-winged orbiter riding on a bigger straight-winged booster. An Air Force laboratory argued that straight wings could not survive the heat and stress of reentry. In January 1971 the two agencies settled on a reusable delta-wing orbiter mounted on a propellant tank that would be thrown away.
